section.title: Final Greetings
section.sectionRationale: Paul closes the letter as he opened it, with peace and grace. He prays that the Lord of peace Himself would give the troubled church peace at all times and in every way, adds his own handwritten signature as a safeguard against the forged letters that had unsettled them, and ends with the grace of the Lord Jesus for all. The benediction gathers up the whole letter's comfort into a few weighty lines.
section.thesis: The Lord of peace Himself is the church's settled hope, giving peace in every circumstance; Paul's own hand authenticates the true apostolic word against every counterfeit, and the letter ends where the gospel always rests, in the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ.
section.frameNote: One brief movement: the prayer for peace from the Lord of peace, the authenticating signature in Paul's own hand, and the closing grace of the Lord Jesus for all.

units.label: Peace, signature, and grace
units.note: the closing benediction of the letter

verses.text: Now may the Lord of {{eirene|peace}} Himself give you peace at all times and in every way. The Lord be with all of you.
This greeting is in my own hand, Paul. This is my {{semeion|mark}} in every letter; it is the way I write.
The {{charis|grace}} of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you.

eirene.gloss: Peace, wholeness, well-being; the Greek word carries the full weight of the Hebrew shalom, a settled flourishing under God. Paul calls the Lord Himself the Lord of peace and prays He would give peace at all times and in every way. For a church rattled by persecution and false alarms, this is peace as a gift of God's own presence, not merely the absence of trouble.

semeion.gloss: A sign, mark, or token of authenticity. Paul points to his own handwriting as the distinguishing mark of a genuine letter in every one he sends. Given the forged or misattributed letter that had alarmed the church, this signature is a safeguard, certifying the true apostolic word against counterfeits.

charis.gloss: Grace, God's undeserved favor and saving kindness. Paul opened the letter with grace and now closes with it, praying the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ on all of them. Grace frames the whole letter, so that even its warnings and commands rest within the free, sustaining favor of Christ.

basic.context: Paul ends his letter the way he began, with peace and grace. To a church shaken by persecution and by a false report that the Day of the Lord had come, he prays that the Lord of peace Himself would give them peace in every situation. He then signs the letter in his own handwriting, a deliberate safeguard because a forged letter had helped cause the confusion he corrected in chapter two. His final word is a blessing of the grace of the Lord Jesus on everyone in the church.
basic.hermeneutics: The closing benediction is more than a formality; each line answers the letter's concerns. The prayer for peace speaks to their anxiety, the signature answers the problem of forged letters, and the grace blessing frames the whole. Reading it well means hearing these lines as the letter's pastoral heartbeat, not skipping them as a routine sign-off.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul calls the Lord the Lord of eirene, peace, the Greek word carrying the full weight of Hebrew shalom, wholeness under God, and prays for it at all times and in every way. He points to his own handwriting as the semeion, the authenticating mark, in every letter, a guard against forgery. He closes with charis, grace, the same word that opened the letter, so grace frames the whole.
basic.typology: The title Lord of peace echoes the Old Testament promise of the Prince of Peace and the LORD who grants shalom to His people. Jesus, the risen Lord, is the giver of that promised peace, present with His church at all times.
basic.christ: Christ is the Lord of peace who gives peace and is present with His people, and the letter ends in the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ. To ask that the Lord be with all of you and that His grace rest on all is to treat the risen Jesus as the ever-present source of peace and favor, a fitting close that centers the whole letter on Him.
basic.god: God is the Lord of peace, personally present with His people and generous with peace in every circumstance. He is a God of grace from the letter's first line to its last, whose favor surrounds even His corrections. The peace and grace He gives are gifts of His own presence, not merely improved circumstances.
basic.crossReferences: First Thessalonians 5 closes with the same prayer that the God of peace would sanctify them wholly. Romans 15 calls Him the God of peace be with you all. And John 14 records Jesus giving His own peace to His troubled disciples, the peace the Lord of peace now grants this church.
basic.oneStory: The letter, and the gospel, rests at last in peace and grace. The Lord of peace who was promised of old and came in Jesus gives His people a settled peace amid every trouble, authenticates His true word against every counterfeit, and surrounds them with grace, a foretaste of the unbroken peace of the new creation where God dwells with His people forever.

context.literary:
These three verses are a closing in the ancient letter form, and each Pauline closing is shaped to its letter. Letters of the time ended with a short wish for health and a farewell, and Paul adapted the form by replacing the farewell with a blessing and by adding, in his own hand, a personal note. In the Thessalonian letters the closings are paired. First Thessalonians ends with the God of peace sanctifying them and a blessing of grace (1 Thessalonians 5:23 to 28). Second Thessalonians ends with the Lord of peace giving peace and a blessing of grace, and adds a notice about the signature, because this letter, unlike the first, has been the subject of forgery.

The structure of the three verses is a small frame. Verse 16 holds two sentences, a prayer for peace and a short statement of presence, 'The Lord be with all of you.' Verse 17 is a note on authentication. Verse 18 is the formal blessing. The last word of verse 16 and the last words of verse 18 are the same, 'all of you,' and the repetition holds the section together. Peace and grace are also the two words of Paul's opening greeting (1:2), so the letter is enclosed between them, and everything between is held inside the Lord's peace and grace.

There is also a link to chapter 3's themes. The 'peace' prayer follows a section in which Paul has dealt with disorder, and the word for peace is placed against the background of the 'undisciplined' life. The peace he asks for is not only a feeling but the right ordering of a community.
context.historical:
In Paul's time letters were commonly dictated to a secretary, who wrote them out, and the sender would add a final line or two in his own hand as a sign of authenticity. We know of this practice from other letters in the New Testament: in Romans 16:22 a man named Tertius says he wrote down the letter, and Paul says 'This greeting is in my own hand' in 1 Corinthians 16:21 and Colossians 4:18. In Galatians 6:11 he calls attention to the size of his own letters, and in Philemon 19 he writes with his own hand to promise repayment. This is the standard feature of his letters, and the claim in 2 Thessalonians 3:17 that this is his 'mark in every letter' shows that he made the habit known.

The reason it appears here with such emphasis is 2:2, where Paul warns against 'a letter seeming to be from us.' In a world without a post office, letters were carried by friends, copied by hand and read aloud in assemblies. A church had few ways to check that a letter was real except by recognizing the sender's hand and the carrier's reputation. By stating that his signature appears at the end of every letter, Paul gives the Thessalonians a way to tell his real letters from false ones.

The peace he prays for was needed. The church was suffering persecution (1:4) and had been unsettled by false teaching (2:2). In a Roman city, 'peace' (pax) was a political promise made by emperors and their propaganda. The apostle's use of 'peace' is a quiet alternative, since it is the Lord's gift, not Rome's.
context.canonical:
The wish for peace has deep roots. It is the heart of the priestly blessing in Numbers 6:24 to 26, which ends 'the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace.' It is the name Gideon gave an altar, 'The LORD Is Peace' (Judges 6:24), and the sign of the covenant that Ezekiel foresees, 'a covenant of peace with them; it will be an everlasting covenant' (Ezekiel 37:26). Isaiah promises that God will keep in perfect peace 'the steadfast of mind' (Isaiah 26:3) and calls the coming child 'Prince of Peace' (Isaiah 9:6).

In the New Testament this peace is given by the risen Christ. Jesus says, 'Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you' (John 14:27), and promises, 'In the world you will have tribulation. But take courage; I have overcome the world!' (John 16:33). Paul says that since we are justified, 'we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ' (Romans 5:1), and that 'He Himself is our peace' (Ephesians 2:14). He prays for the same gift in several closings: 'The God of peace be with all of you' (Romans 15:33), 'The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet' (Romans 16:20), and in Hebrews, 'the God of peace, who through the blood of the eternal covenant brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus' (Hebrews 13:20).

The grace blessing is the standard apostolic farewell, and the New Testament itself ends with it: 'The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all the saints. Amen' (Revelation 22:21). The effect of these two endings, one at the end of a small letter and one at the end of the whole Bible, is that Scripture closes the way Paul's letters close, with the grace of the Lord Jesus.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul meant this closing to settle the church, not just to say goodbye. After a letter that dealt with persecution, a panic about the end, a prophecy of lawlessness and a rebuke of the idle, he does not want them to leave with a sense of unresolved threat. He wants them to leave with the peace of the Lord, in every circumstance and at every time. The prayer is not that trouble will vanish but that peace will be given 'in every way,' including through it.

The reference to his own hand has a protective purpose. Forged letters had already done damage, and Paul wanted to prevent more. He does this simply: he states what he always does, so that the church has a test to apply.

And the last words, 'with all of you,' are a message to the whole church, including the idle he has just rebuked and the ones he has told to be shamed. The offender is not left outside the blessing. By repeating 'all' in verses 16 and 18, Paul reminds the church that the discipline of verses 14 and 15 is inside the fellowship of grace. The care that sent the warning also sends the blessing, and it asks the church to hear them together.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The closing is mostly prayer and report. Verses 16 and 18 are wishes addressed to the Lord on behalf of the church. Verse 17 reports what Paul does and gives the reason. None of these is a command in the ordinary sense. They show us what to ask for and what grounds to give, not what to do.

Still there are things we can learn to practice. We can learn to end our own words to one another with real blessing, and to pray specifically for peace in the places where there is anxiety. We can learn to treat the signed word of a trusted teacher as a safeguard against falsehood, and to test what claims apostolic authority against the apostolic writings. And we can take the last line as a model for how to speak to those who have been disciplined: with 'all of you.'

What the passage does not do is give a formula, such as a required liturgy, or turn Paul's handwriting into a rule about handwritten letters. The signature was a way to deal with forged documents in the first century, and its modern analog is the discipline of checking a source before passing it on. The enduring principle is that the church's confidence rests on a testified, reliable word.

debates.question: Does the signature in verse 17 settle whether Paul wrote 2 Thessalonians?

views.label: Yes, Paul wrote it, with a secretary
views.case: The letter claims Paul's authorship in 1:1 and again here, with a personal mark, and the church's reception of it from the earliest centuries supports the claim. The style, the concerns and the closing match 1 Thessalonians and Paul's habit in 1 Corinthians 16:21 and Colossians 4:18. The differences from the first letter are explained by a changed situation and the fact that this is a corrective letter.

views.label: A later writer in Paul's name
views.case: Some scholars question Pauline authorship because of the more formal tone and what they see as a different picture of the end. On this view the line about 'my own hand' is part of the later writer's attempt to give the letter authority, and it shows that forged letters were a real concern.

views.label: Paul wrote it, but the signature settles only what it says
views.case: A cautious approach notes that a signature authenticates a document only to those who know the hand. The note is an argument to its first readers, not a proof to us, and our confidence comes from the whole case: external attestation and internal consistency.

debates.bearing: The claim in verse 17 is clear and Christians have received the letter as Paul's from the start. What the passage gives us is not a proof but an example of how the apostle protected his word, and why a church can trust what it has received.

debates.question: Who is 'the Lord of peace,' and does the wish mean peace within or peace around?

views.label: The Lord Jesus Christ
views.case: In this letter 'the Lord' normally means Jesus (for example 1:1, 2:1, 3:6), and the blessing in verse 18 names 'our Lord Jesus Christ.' Isaiah calls the coming child the 'Prince of Peace' (Isaiah 9:6), and Paul says 'He Himself is our peace' (Ephesians 2:14). The title would then give Jesus a role the Old Testament gives to God.

views.label: God the Father
views.case: Elsewhere Paul regularly uses 'the God of peace' (Romans 15:33; 16:20; Philippians 4:9; 1 Thessalonians 5:23), and 'Lord' may be a loose reference here to the same person. The prayer in 2:16 had both Jesus and the Father in view.

views.label: The undivided Lord who gives the peace of both Father and Son
views.case: A third view holds that Paul does not separate the persons, since in this letter the Father and Son share one verb (2:16 to 17) and one source of grace and peace (1:2). On that view, the title belongs to the Lord whose work is one.

debates.bearing: The most natural reading, in a letter that uses 'Lord' for Jesus, is that Paul calls Christ 'Lord of peace.' Even if the Father is meant, the New Testament does not hesitate to say that the peace of God comes through Christ, so the practical meaning is the same.

study.originalLanguages:
The title in verse 16, 'the Lord of peace,' is unusual in Paul. His usual phrase is 'the God of peace,' as in Romans 15:33, Romans 16:20, Philippians 4:9 and 1 Thessalonians 5:23. Here he changes the title to 'the Lord,' which in this letter regularly means Jesus. The word for peace is eirene, and behind it stands the Hebrew shalom, which means wholeness and well-being, not just the absence of conflict. When Paul prays that peace be given 'at all times and in every way,' he is asking for a gift that reaches into every circumstance.

The last phrase offers a small puzzle. Many manuscripts read en panti tropo, 'in every way,' as the English text has it, while a number read en panti topo, 'in every place.' The two readings differ by one letter. The meaning is close, since peace in every way and peace in every place both cover the whole of life, and either way Paul prays that the peace he asks for is not limited to good times or to certain situations. The 'at all times' that comes before it, dia pantos, is literally 'through all,' that is continually.

The verb 'give' is the aorist optative, doie, a form used for a wish: 'may He give.' It places the whole sentence as a prayer, and the word 'Himself,' autos, is a strong pronoun: the Lord Himself, not an agent or an idea. Paul uses the same emphatic 'Himself' in 2:16 and in 1 Thessalonians 5:23, so that the gift is thought of as coming straight from the Lord's own hand.

The short sentence 'The Lord be with all of you' uses the same preposition as the closing blessing, meta, 'with,' and the same 'all of you,' pantōn hymōn. Paul echoes his own wording in verse 18, and in doing so he binds the peace and the grace to the same assembly: all of you, including those he has just corrected.

In verse 17 the word is semeion, 'sign' or 'mark,' the word used in the gospels for signs that point to something. Paul says that this is the sign in every letter, and 'the way I write,' houtos grapho, literally 'so I write.' This is the language of authentication. The word used here for 'greeting' is aspasmos, a word that can mean a simple hello, and is here used for the whole closing. It matters that Paul says 'in my own hand,' te eme cheiri, and puts his own name, Paul, at the end of the clause, as a signature.

typology.fulfillment: In Numbers 6:24 to 26 the priests were to bless Israel in the LORD's name, ending with peace: the LORD 'give you peace.' The apostle's closing is a priestly act in a new key, spoken over a church by an apostle who has no temple. The correspondence is the pattern of a spoken blessing that places the LORD's name on His people. The escalation is that the blessing comes from the risen Lord Jesus, who is both the one who blesses and the peace given (Ephesians 2:14). The type falls short because Aaron's blessing was a wish spoken over a nation under a covenant not yet fulfilled; Paul's blessing is spoken over those who already have peace with God (Romans 5:1).

typology.type: The name of the altar, 'The LORD Is Peace'
typology.fulfillment: Gideon, afraid he would die after seeing the angel of the LORD, was told 'Peace to you' and built an altar called The LORD Is Peace (Judges 6:23 to 24). Peace there was not a mood but a name for God Himself. The correspondence is the idea that peace belongs to the LORD and is given by Him. The escalation is that in Paul's prayer the title is given to Jesus, 'the Lord of peace,' who is Himself the place where God and His people meet. The type falls short in that Gideon's peace was a reassurance in the face of danger from the holiness of God, while the peace of Christ is the removal of that danger by His death.

God promised through Ezekiel, 'I will make a covenant of peace with them; it will be an everlasting covenant' (Ezekiel 37:26), and through Isaiah, 'Peace, peace to those far and near' (Isaiah 57:19). Paul's prayer assumes that the covenant has arrived in Christ. The correspondence is the promise of lasting wholeness for a restored people. The escalation is that this peace now reaches the Gentiles, who were 'far,' and is given by the Spirit to believers (Ephesians 2:17). The type falls short of the final form, since the full peace of the covenant, with no more enemies, waits for the new creation.

typology.type: The sealed word of a trusted messenger
typology.fulfillment: Throughout Scripture, a word is authenticated by its source: the prophet's 'Thus says the LORD,' the king's seal, the apostle's mark. Paul's note about his handwriting belongs in this line. The correspondence is a community's reliance on a word that can be verified. The escalation is that the apostolic word carries the authority of Christ (Matthew 28:20, 'teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you'), and the Spirit guides the apostles into the truth (John 16:13). The type falls short in that handwriting is only a human sign; the ultimate assurance that a word is the Lord's comes through the Spirit's testimony.

study.christ:
The closing of this letter does what the whole letter does: it puts Christ in the place of every anxiety. Notice first the title. In the closing prayer it is the Lord, not an angel or an idea, who 'Himself' gives peace. The Old Testament gave this role to the LORD alone: He is the one who gives peace (Numbers 6:26) and the one whose name is peace (Judges 6:24). Paul now assigns the same role to Jesus. This is not argued; it is simply assumed in a blessing, which makes it all the more telling.

Second, peace in the New Testament is not an abstraction. It is a Person who made it. Jesus said, 'Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives' (John 14:27). He gave it on the eve of His death, and He gave it again after His resurrection, when He met His frightened disciples with the greeting 'Peace be with you.' Paul can say that 'He Himself is our peace' (Ephesians 2:14) because the cross removed the hostility between God and us, and between Jew and Gentile. When the apostle prays that the Lord of peace give peace, he is praying that the people who are already at peace with God by the cross would also have the felt, daily peace that flows from it. That is why Romans 5:1 says 'we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.' The peace was won by Christ and is now given by Him.

Third, the words 'The Lord be with all of you' echo the promise of the risen Christ at the close of the Great Commission: 'I am with you always, even to the end of the age' (Matthew 28:20). It shows that the church of Thessalonica, scattered and shaken, was not left to itself. The One who ascended is present with His people. This is the answer to the question of verse 2, whether the Lord had come: He is present now by His Spirit, and will come in glory later.

Fourth, the closing blessing is a statement of grace, and grace in Paul is a person-centered word. 'The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ' means the favor that Jesus embodies and gives, for 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor' (2 Corinthians 8:9). Everything the letter has asked of them, to stand firm, to work, to do good and to stay at peace, rests on that grace and is made possible by it.
study.god:
The God of this closing is a God who is present. The simple sentence 'The Lord be with all of you' is easy to pass over, but it names the most important thing a church can have. Theology says that God is everywhere, but the Bible's promise is more particular: He is with His people. He promised Moses His presence at the burning bush, and the name Immanuel, 'God with us,' sums up the hope (Matthew 1:23). Paul's closing is a prayer that this particular, covenant presence be known by everyone in the church, as peace and as grace.

God is the source of peace and not only its sponsor. The title 'Lord of peace' says that peace is His to give, and the prayer 'give you peace' says that He gives it freely. This is a different picture from a God who is merely calm; He is the one who produces peace in people, at all times and in every way. Isaiah says that He keeps in perfect peace those whose minds are steadfast because they trust Him (Isaiah 26:3), and Paul says elsewhere that the peace of God 'will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus' (Philippians 4:7). The word 'guard' is a military term, a sentry at the door. The peace of God is a defense.

God is also a God of grace from the first line of the letter to the last. The opening (1:2) is 'Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ,' and the close is 'The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ.' Grace means that all He does for His people is unearned. A letter with strong warnings and sharp commands does not abandon this foundation; it begins and ends on it. The order is itself a doctrine: grace is the frame and the ground, and obedience is the response.

There is a tension that the closing leaves in place and does not apologize for. God is the Lord of peace, and yet the letter has described persecution, a coming rebellion and a delusion sent in judgment. God's peace does not mean there is no trouble; it means that trouble does not have the last word. Jesus said, 'In the world you will have tribulation. But take courage; I have overcome the world' (John 16:33).

For worship, this means that the church can end its gatherings the way Paul ended his letter: with a blessing that is not wishful thinking but a prayer to the Lord who is able. And it means that the believer's own sense of peace has a source outside himself, which is why it can survive circumstances that would otherwise shake it.

crossReferences.note: 'May the God of peace Himself sanctify you completely.' This is the first letter's closing prayer, with the same emphatic 'Himself.' It shows that peace in Paul's closings is tied to holiness and to being kept blameless at Christ's coming.

'The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet.' Peace here is a victory over an enemy, not a mood. It reminds us that the peace Paul prays for stands against spiritual opposition and is strong enough to withstand it.

The peace of God 'will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.' It adds that the peace is a guard, and it is found 'in Christ Jesus.' It explains how the peace of 2 Thessalonians 3:16 can hold in times of anxiety.

'Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives.' The source of the peace Paul asks for. The Lord who gives it is the Lord who spoke these words before the cross.

The priestly blessing, ending with 'give you peace.' Paul's closing carries on this form of blessing. The same sequence runs through the blessing: the LORD blesses and keeps, shows favor and is gracious, and finally gives peace, so that peace is the last and summing-up gift.

Gideon names an altar 'The LORD Is Peace.' The verse shows that in Israel peace could be a name of God Himself, set on an altar after a frightened man was told he would live. That is the background to Paul's title 'Lord of peace,' which treats peace as belonging to a person.
The promised child is called 'Prince of Peace.' Paul's 'Lord of peace' is the New Testament recognition that the child has come and has the title, in the risen Jesus who gives peace to His people.
'He Himself is our peace, who has made the two one.' It explains what kind of peace the Lord of peace gives: peace with God and with others, based on His own person and the cross.
'We have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.' It describes the settled fact beneath the prayer. The peace Paul asks for 'at all times' is built on a peace already made.
'This greeting is in my own hand, Paul.' The same personal note in a different letter. It shows that the handwriting note in 2 Thessalonians 3:17 is a regular practice, not a one-off response.

'This greeting is in my own hand, Paul. Remember my chains. Grace be with you.' Another letter with the same closing note and the same grace blessing. It shows that the pattern in 2 Thessalonians 3:17 and 18 is typical.
'See what large letters I am using to write to you with my own hand!' Another case of Paul pointing to his own handwriting, which supports the claim that a personal hand at the end was his habit.
'The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all the saints.' The Bible's last verse closes as Paul's letters do. It places 2 Thessalonians 3:18 in a pattern that runs to the end of Scripture.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with a world that is 'very good' and with peace in every direction: between God and humanity, between husband and wife, between people and the ground. The fall broke all of these, and the story that follows is the long work of restoring peace. The word that names that restoration is shalom, and the New Testament's closings, including this one, are the way the apostles keep that word alive in the life of the church.

Consider what this ending answers from before. The priests of Israel blessed the people with peace, and the people kept hoping for a covenant of peace that would last (Ezekiel 37:26). The prophets spoke of a child who would be Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6) and of a peace that would reach those who were far off (Isaiah 57:19). The Thessalonians, who were Gentiles, had been among the 'far off.' Paul's prayer that the Lord of peace Himself give them peace is evidence that the promise had arrived.

Consider what it sets up. The prayer for peace 'at all times and in every way' looks ahead to the troubles the church will face: more persecution, more false teaching, more disorder. Peace is given as a resource for the long road between the first coming of Christ and the second. And the grace that closes the letter is the grace that carries the church through that road.

And consider how it ends. The last book of the Bible gives the picture of a world where the curse is gone, where God dwells with His people, and where they see His face (Revelation 22:3 to 4). The peace that the Lord gives now is a first installment of that. It is why Paul can pray for peace in the middle of persecution without sounding naive: the peace is a pledge of the end.

The signature has its own place in the story. From the beginning God's people have asked how they can know that a word is really His. Here the answer is a person's handwriting; in the larger story it is the testimony of the apostles, the Scriptures they left, and the Spirit who confirms them. The church that holds these is secure against forgeries of every kind. The story closes on grace, as this letter does: the whole account from Eden to the new creation is the story of the grace of the Lord Jesus, given to all.

quiz.q: What does Paul pray for the church in verse 16?

options.text: That the Lord of peace Himself would give them peace at all times and in every way.
options.note: Verse 16 prays for peace from the Lord of peace in every circumstance.

options.text: That they would finally get revenge on their persecutors.
options.note: The prayer is for peace, not revenge.

options.text: That they would become wealthy and untroubled.
options.note: The peace prayed for is God's gift in every circumstance, not material ease.

options.text: That they would be left to find peace on their own.
options.note: The peace comes from the Lord of peace Himself, not from their own efforts.

quiz.q: Why does Paul add a greeting in his own hand in verse 17?

options.text: As a mark of authenticity in every letter, guarding against forged letters.
options.note: Verse 17 gives his handwriting as the distinguishing mark against counterfeits.

options.text: Because he did not trust anyone else to deliver the letter.
options.note: The point is authentication of the letter itself, not distrust of a courier.

options.text: To show off his handwriting skill.
options.note: The signature is a safeguard of authenticity, not a display.

options.text: Because he had forgotten to sign his other letters.
options.note: He says this mark appears in every letter; it is a deliberate practice, not an oversight.

quiz.q: How does the letter end, in verse 18?

options.text: With the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you.
options.note: Verse 18 closes with the grace of Christ for all, framing the letter.

options.text: With a stern final warning of judgment.
options.note: The letter ends on grace, not on a warning.

options.text: With a list of names to be excluded.
options.note: It ends with grace for all of you, not with exclusion.
The close is a grace-benediction, not a financial appeal.

quiz.q: What does the title Lord of peace, with the emphatic Himself, stress in verse 16?

options.text: That true peace comes from the personal presence of the Lord.
options.note: The emphatic Himself points to peace flowing from the Lord's own presence.

options.text: That peace is merely the absence of external conflict.
options.note: The biblical peace is fuller wholeness rooted in the Lord, not just calm circumstances.

options.text: That the church must manufacture its own peace.
options.note: Peace is the Lord's gift, given by His presence, not self-manufactured.

options.text: That peace will only come after death.
options.note: He gives peace at all times and in every way, now as well as forever.

questions: Paul prays for peace at all times and in every way from the Lord of peace Himself. In what circumstance right now do you most need to receive peace as a gift of the Lord's presence rather than a change in your situation?

The whole letter is framed by grace, from its opening line to its last. How does knowing that even God's warnings and commands come wrapped in His grace change the way you read hard passages of Scripture?

Paul guarded the church against counterfeit messages by pointing to the authentic apostolic word. How do you test the many voices and messages competing for your attention against the trustworthy Scriptures?

The letter ends with a blessing of grace on all of you, not a select few. Who in your church family most needs to hear that the grace of the Lord Jesus is genuinely for them, and how could you tell them?

translationNotes.note: The Lord of peace renders a title that draws on the Hebrew idea of shalom, wholeness and flourishing under God; the emphatic Himself stresses that peace comes from the Lord's own presence.
This greeting is in my own hand, Paul reflects Paul's practice of adding a handwritten note to a dictated letter; here it serves to authenticate the letter against forgery.
Some later manuscripts (BYZ and TR) add Amen at the end; the BSB follows the earlier reading without it.
